people.name: Hiero II
people.summary: Tyrant then king of Syracuse (c. 270-215) who fought Rome in 264, switched to alliance in 263, and stayed loyal for half a century, supplying grain and money. His tithe law (lex Hieronica) became the basis of Roman taxation of Sicily; Archimedes was his kinsman and engineer.

people.name: Archimedes
people.summary: The greatest mathematician of antiquity, whose war machines held Marcellus at bay during the siege of Syracuse; killed by a Roman soldier in the sack of 212, reportedly while drawing figures in the sand. Cicero found his tomb, marked with a sphere inscribed in a cylinder, in 75 BC.
people.death: killed by a Roman soldier during the sack of Syracuse

people.name: Hannibal son of Gisco
people.summary: Carthaginian commander who defended Agrigentum (262-261), captured Scipio Asina at Lipara (260) but lost at Mylae; crucified by his own officers after the defeat off Sulci (258).
people.death: crucified by his own men in Sardinia

people.name: Xanthippus
people.summary: Spartan mercenary officer who reorganised the Carthaginian army and destroyed Regulus at Tunes (255), then left Carthage; later stories of his murder by jealous Carthaginians are dubious.

people.name: Adherbal
people.summary: Carthaginian admiral who destroyed Publius Claudius Pulcher's fleet at Drepana in 249, the only great Carthaginian naval victory of the war.

people.name: Carthalo
people.summary: Carthaginian admiral who in 249 harried the Roman convoy of Junius Pullus and manoeuvred it onto a lee shore where a storm destroyed it; raided the Italian coast in 248.

people.name: Hamilcar Barca
people.summary: Father of Hannibal, Hasdrubal and Mago. Undefeated commander in Sicily (247-241) at Heircte and Eryx, saviour of Carthage in the Mercenary War, and founder of the Barcid dominion in Spain from 237, where he drowned in 229/228. His nickname Barca probably means 'lightning'.
people.detail: Polybius (3.9-10) makes 'the wrath of Hamilcar', inflamed by the loss of Sardinia, the first cause of the Second Punic War, a view now often thought too personal. Hoyos sees him as building a Barcid power base in Spain in cooperation with the home government.
people.death: drowned crossing a river while retreating from Helice

people.name: Hanno the Great

roles.t: General in Africa and in the Mercenary War

people.summary: Leader of the landed aristocracy at Carthage and rival of the Barcids; conqueror of territory in Africa, initially unsuccessful commander in the Mercenary War, and in Roman tradition the advocate of peace with Rome who opposed Hannibal's war.
people.debate: Livy's speeches of Hanno against the Barcids may reflect Roman interpretations more than Carthaginian politics.

people.name: Mathos
people.summary: Libyan soldier who with Spendius led the mercenary and Libyan revolt against Carthage (241-238); after his defeat he was dragged through the streets of Carthage and tortured to death.
people.death: executed at Carthage after a triumph-like procession

people.name: Hasdrubal the Fair
people.summary: Son-in-law of Hamilcar Barca and his successor in Spain (229-221), who expanded Carthaginian power by diplomacy and marriage to an Iberian princess, founded New Carthage and concluded the Ebro treaty with Rome. Murdered by a Celt.
people.death: assassinated by a Celtic servant at New Carthage

people.name: Hannibal Barca
people.summary: Rome's most dangerous enemy. Commander in Spain from 221, he took Saguntum, crossed the Alps in 218 and destroyed Roman armies at the Trebia, Trasimene and Cannae, then held out in southern Italy for thirteen more years until recalled to Africa and defeated by Scipio at Zama (202). As suffete (196) he reformed Carthage's finances and courts, then fled to Antiochus III, lost a naval battle at the Eurymedon, and finally took poison in Bithynia to avoid extradition.
people.detail: Polybius admired his generalship and noted that his multi-ethnic army never mutinied in sixteen years; Livy portrays him as brilliant but cruel and faithless ('perfidia plus quam Punica'). Modern debate centres on his strategy: whether he expected Rome's Italian alliance to collapse after Cannae, why he did not march on Rome, and whether his grand strategy was ever realistic given Roman manpower (Lazenby, Goldsworthy, Hoyos, Lancel). No portrait is certainly identified, though Barcid coins from Spain may show him.
people.death: suicide by poison at Libyssa, Bithynia, to avoid extradition to Rome

people.name: Hasdrubal Barca
people.summary: Hannibal's younger brother, commander in Spain from 218, defeated by the Scipios at Dertosa (215) but victorious over them in 211; checked by Africanus at Baecula (208), he slipped away to Italy across the Alps and was destroyed and killed at the Metaurus (207).
people.death: killed at the Metaurus; his head thrown into Hannibal's camp

people.name: Mago Barca
people.summary: Youngest brother of Hannibal; led the ambush at the Trebia, fought at Cannae and brought news of it to Carthage, served in Spain (211-206), held Minorca (Port Mahón bears his name), landed at Genua (205) and died of wounds on the voyage home in 203.
people.death: died of a thigh wound at sea off Sardinia
people.debate: Nepos and Zonaras report a different end.

people.name: Hasdrubal son of Gisco
people.summary: Carthaginian commander in Spain (214-206) who shared in the defeat of the Scipios (211) and lost at Ilipa (206); father of Sophonisba, he won Syphax for Carthage but lost both their armies to Scipio's night attack and at the Great Plains (203). He committed suicide or was killed by a mob in 202.

people.name: Hanno son of Bomilcar
people.summary: Hannibal's nephew (Appian) and officer who outflanked the Volcae at the Rhône crossing (218), probably commanded the right at Cannae, and fought the Romans in southern Italy, losing at Beneventum (214).
people.debate: It is not certain that all actions attributed to 'Hanno' in southern Italy belong to the same man.

people.name: Maharbal
people.summary: Hannibal's cavalry commander who captured the Roman vanguard after Trasimene and destroyed Centenius' cavalry; Livy has him tell Hannibal after Cannae, 'you know how to win, not how to use a victory'.
people.debate: The famous remark appears only in Livy and may be invented; Polybius gives Maharbal no such role at Cannae.

people.name: Hasdrubal (Cannae)
people.summary: Commander of Hannibal's Spanish and Celtic heavy cavalry on the left at Cannae, who routed the Roman horse, rode behind the Roman army to scatter the allied cavalry and then charged the rear of the legions.

people.name: Hasdrubal the Boetharch
people.summary: Carthaginian general defeated by Masinissa in 150 and condemned to death to appease Rome, then recalled to lead the defence of Carthage (149-146). He tortured Roman prisoners on the walls, surrendered on the Byrsa and was spared to live in Italy; his wife killed herself and their children.

people.name: Sophonisba
people.fullName: Sophonisba (Saphanba'al) daughter of Hasdrubal son of Gisco
people.summary: Carthaginian noblewoman married to Syphax to bind him to Carthage; after his capture she married Masinissa, who, ordered by Scipio to give her up as a captive, sent her poison, which she drank.
people.death: poison sent by Masinissa

people.name: Syphax
people.summary: King of the western Numidian Masaesylii, courted by both Rome and Carthage; married Sophonisba and sided with Carthage, lost his army in Scipio's night attack (203) and was captured by Laelius and Masinissa. He died a prisoner in Italy.
people.death: died in captivity at Tibur (Livy) or after Scipio's triumph (Polybius)

people.name: Masinissa
people.summary: Massylian prince who fought for Carthage in Spain, switched to Rome in 206, helped win the Great Plains and Zama, and was made king of all Numidia. For fifty years he used the 201 treaty to annex Carthaginian territory, provoking the Third Punic War. He fathered a son at 86 and led his army at 88; Scipio Aemilianus divided his kingdom among his sons.
people.detail: Polybius (36.16) admired his vigour and claimed he transformed Numidia into a land of settled agriculture, though archaeology suggests agriculture was already established. His monumental tomb is perhaps the Medracen or El-Khroub mausoleum near Cirta.

people.name: Indibilis
people.summary: Chief of the Ilergetes of north-east Spain, captured at Cissa (218), then a shifting ally of Carthage and Rome; with his brother Mandonius he revolted against Scipio in 206 and was killed in battle in 205.
people.death: killed in battle against the Romans

people.name: Teuta
people.summary: Widow of King Agron and regent of the Illyrian kingdom whose fleets raided Epirus and the Adriatic; Rome's war on her in 229-228 brought Roman armies to the Balkans for the first time. Polybius' portrait of her as an irrational woman is hostile.

people.name: Demetrius of Pharos
people.summary: Greek-Illyrian dynast who betrayed Corcyra to Rome in 229, was rewarded with a principality, then defied Rome and was driven out in 219. At Philip V's court he urged war on Rome; he was killed attacking Messene in 214.
people.death: killed in an assault on Messene

people.name: Genthius
people.summary: Last Ardiaean king (c. 181-168), who allied with Perseus for a subsidy that never fully arrived and was conquered by Anicius in thirty days; led in triumph and interned at Iguvium.

people.name: Viridomarus
people.summary: King of the Gaesatae killed in single combat by Marcellus at Clastidium (222), whose armour was dedicated as the last spolia opima.
people.death: killed by Marcellus at Clastidium

people.name: Aneroestes
people.summary: King of the Gaesatae who with Concolitanus led the great Gallic invasion of 225; after Telamon he fled and killed himself with his companions.
people.death: suicide after Telamon

people.name: Philip V
people.summary: Antigonid king of Macedon (221-179), the 'darling of Greece' turned tyrant in Polybius' account. He allied with Hannibal (215), fought Rome in the First (214-205) and Second (200-197) Macedonian Wars, was beaten at Cynoscephalae, and then cooperated with Rome against Antiochus while quietly rebuilding his kingdom. His last years were darkened by the execution of his son Demetrius.
people.detail: Polybius traces his moral decline from 215 (the sack of Messene, the advice of Demetrius of Pharos). Walbank's biography reassessed him as an able ruler whose ambitions collided with Rome's emerging hegemony.

people.name: Perseus
people.summary: Last king of Macedon (179-168). Popular among Greek commoners and allied by marriage to the Seleucids, he alarmed Rome and Eumenes; defeated at Pydna (168), he surrendered at Samothrace, walked in Paullus' triumph and died in captivity at Alba Fucens.
people.death: died in captivity at Alba Fucens, perhaps by starvation or sleep deprivation

people.name: Andriscus
people.summary: Fuller from Adramyttium who claimed to be a son of Perseus, seized Macedonia with Thracian help in 149, killed a Roman praetor and was defeated by Metellus in 148; led in Metellus' triumph and executed.
people.death: executed after Metellus' triumph

people.name: Antiochus III
people.summary: Seleucid king (222-187) who lost at Raphia (217), restored the empire's eastern satrapies in his anabasis (212-205), took Coele-Syria at Panium (200), and crossed into Europe. Invited by the Aetolians, he fought Rome and was defeated at Thermopylae (191) and Magnesia (190/189); by the Treaty of Apamea he lost Asia Minor and paid 15,000 talents. Killed plundering a temple in Elymais.
people.detail: Polybius thought him vigorous in youth and feeble in age. Grainger and others see his war with Rome as a misjudgement born of a different understanding of legitimate spheres, not a planned bid for world power.
people.death: killed by locals while robbing the temple of Bel in Elymais
scholarship: Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (2002)

people.name: Antiochus IV Epiphanes
people.summary: Son of Antiochus III, hostage in Rome after Apamea, king from 175. He conquered most of Egypt in the Sixth Syrian War until the Roman envoy Popillius Laenas drew a circle round him at Eleusis (168). His suppression of Jewish worship in Jerusalem provoked the Maccabean revolt.

people.name: Demetrius I Soter
people.summary: Son of Seleucus IV, hostage in Rome from 178, who escaped in 162 with Polybius' help and seized the Seleucid throne; killed fighting the Roman-backed pretender Alexander Balas.

people.name: Ptolemy IV Philopator
people.summary: King of Egypt (221-204), victor over Antiochus III at Raphia (217) with an army including 20,000 native Egyptian phalangites; Polybius depicts him as dissolute, ruled by his ministers Sosibius and Agathocles.

people.name: Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II
people.summary: Younger brother and rival of Ptolemy VI, king of Cyrene from 163 and of Egypt from 145; in 155 he published a will leaving Cyrene to Rome, the first known royal bequest to the Roman people. Scipio Aemilianus' embassy saw him in 139 and mocked his corpulence.

people.name: Attalus I
people.summary: King of Pergamon (241-197) who won fame by defeating the Galatians, allied with Rome against Philip V, bought Aegina, helped bring the Magna Mater to Rome and urged the Second Macedonian War; he collapsed while addressing the Boeotians and died soon after.

people.name: Eumenes II
people.summary: King of Pergamon (197-159), Rome's chief ally in Asia, whose cavalry and light troops decided Magnesia and who gained most of Seleucid Asia Minor at Apamea; builder of the Great Altar and library of Pergamon. He denounced Perseus at Rome (172) but lost Roman favour after 168.

people.name: Attalus III
people.summary: Last Attalid king (138-133), reputed by hostile sources to have neglected government for botany, poisons and sculpture; on his death he bequeathed his kingdom to the Roman people.

people.name: Aristonicus
people.summary: Illegitimate son of Eumenes II who claimed the Attalid throne after the bequest of 133, minted coins as Eumenes III and rallied the poor and slaves as 'Heliopolitans'; defeated the consul Crassus Mucianus (130) but was captured by Perperna and strangled in a Roman prison.
people.death: strangled in prison at Rome

people.name: Nabis
people.summary: Last independent king of Sparta (207-192), a revolutionary who freed helots and redistributed property; Rome and the Achaeans warred on him in 195. Murdered by the Aetolians in 192.
people.death: assassinated by the Aetolian Alexamenus

people.name: Philopoemen
people.summary: Eight times strategos of the Achaean League, who reformed its army on Macedonian lines, killed the Spartan tyrant Machanidas at Mantinea (207), annexed Sparta (192) and tried to keep the League independent of Rome; called 'the last of the Greeks'. Captured and poisoned by the Messenians.
people.death: forced to drink poison by the Messenians

people.name: Polybius
people.fullName: Polybius son of Lycortas, of Megalopolis
people.summary: Achaean statesman and cavalry commander (169) deported to Rome as a hostage in 167, where he became mentor to Scipio Aemilianus. He witnessed the destruction of Carthage (146) and helped reorganise Greece after the fall of Corinth. His Histories, in 40 books (1-5 complete), explained how Rome came to dominate the known world in under 53 years (220-167) and is the main source for this whole era.
people.detail: Polybius insisted on autopsy (he walked Hannibal's route over the Alps), documents (he read the Rome-Carthage treaties and Hannibal's Lacinian inscription) and political experience, and attacked rivals such as Timaeus, Phylarchus and Fabius Pictor. His analysis of the Roman 'mixed constitution' (book 6) and his comparison of legion and phalanx (book 18) are foundational. His closeness to the Scipios and his Achaean loyalties colour his judgements; Livy used him extensively for eastern affairs, sometimes translating him almost word for word.
people.death: said to have died at 82 after a fall from his horse
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius, 3 vols (1957-1979)
Eckstein, Moral Vision in the Histories of Polybius (1995)

people.name: Critolaus
people.summary: Achaean strategos in 147/146 who rejected Roman demands, suspended debt collection and led the League into war with Rome; vanished after his defeat at Scarpheia.
people.death: disappeared after Scarpheia, perhaps drowned or by poison

people.name: Diaeus
people.summary: Achaean strategos who succeeded Critolaus in 146, freed and armed slaves, and was defeated by Mummius at Leucopetra; he killed his wife and poisoned himself at Megalopolis.
people.death: suicide by poison

people.name: Carneades
people.summary: Head of the sceptical New Academy at Athens, whose lectures for and against justice during the embassy of 155 dazzled Roman youth and alarmed Cato.

people.name: Diogenes of Babylon
people.summary: Head of the Stoa at Athens and member of the philosophers' embassy of 155; teacher of Panaetius, who later brought Stoicism into the circle of Scipio Aemilianus.

people.name: Critolaus of Phaselis
people.summary: Head of the Peripatetic school at Athens and member of the philosophers' embassy to Rome in 155; not to be confused with the Achaean general of 146.

people.name: Judas Maccabaeus
people.summary: Leader of the Jewish revolt against the Seleucids from 166, who rededicated the Temple in Jerusalem (164, the origin of Hanukkah) and concluded a treaty of friendship with Rome (161); killed at Elasa in 160.
people.death: killed in battle at Elasa

people.name: Viriathus
people.summary: Lusitanian shepherd and survivor of Galba's massacre (150) who led a guerrilla war from 147 to 139, defeating a series of Roman praetors and consuls and forcing Fabius Servilianus to recognise him as a friend of the Roman people (140). Murdered by his own envoys, bribed by Caepio.
people.detail: Diodorus (33.1, 7, 21), following Posidonius, idealises him as a man of simple virtue. He became a national hero of Portugal and Spain.
people.death: stabbed in his sleep by three of his envoys bribed by Q. Servilius Caepio

people.name: Eunus
people.summary: Syrian slave from Apamea owned at Enna, a prophet and wonder-worker who led the great Sicilian slave revolt from c. 135, took the royal name Antiochus and minted coins; captured in 132, he died in prison at Morgantina.
people.death: died in prison at Morgantina
